question_text: Prove that the roots of (x − a)(x − b) = h² are always real.

Δ = (a − b)² + (2h)² is ≥ 0, and equals 0 when a = b and h = 0 (equal real roots), so the honest line is Δ ≥ 0; the printed conclusion 'roots are real' is still correct.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove the roots are always real — say what you expand to, what you compute, and why it can never be negative.
insider_note: Move h² across before computing Δ — the constant becomes ab − h², which is what the proof needs. Write Δ as (a − b)² + (2h)²: a sum of two squares is never negative, and that visible form is the whole argument.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write as a quadratic
steps.margin_note: First mark. Expand the left side and move h² across: x² − (a + b)x + (ab − h²) = 0. The constant term is ab − h², and that minus sign is what the proof uses.
steps.memory_tip: Move h² across before reading Δ: the constant is ab − h², and that minus is what the proof uses.

recall.must_convey: That the equation is expanded and rearranged to the standard form x² − (a + b)x + (ab − h²) = 0.
accept: expand the brackets and bring h squared to the left to get x squared minus a plus b x plus a b minus h squared
write it as a quadratic with coefficients one, minus a plus b, and a b minus h squared
put it in the form x squared minus sum times x plus product minus h squared equals zero
brackets expand chesi h squared ni left ki techi standard form lo rayali

steps.why: The discriminant test only applies to the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, so the equation must be rearranged before Δ can be read off.
common_mistakes: Leaving h² on the right and using c = ab.
Writing the x coefficient as +(a + b).
Expanding (x − a)(x − b) as x² − abx + ab.

steps.label: Δ ≥ 0
steps.mark_note: Δ is a sum of squares
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Δ = (a + b)² − 4ab + 4h² = (a − b)² + 4h². Write 4h² as (2h)² so it is visibly a square. A sum of two squares is never negative, so Δ ≥ 0 for every a, b, h — that IS the proof.
steps.memory_tip: (a + b)² − 4ab = (a − b)². Write 4h² as (2h)² so Δ is visibly a sum of two squares.
lines: (a sum of two squares is never negative)

recall.must_convey: That Δ = (a + b)² − 4(ab − h²) simplifies to (a − b)² + (2h)², a sum of two squares, so Δ ≥ 0 and the roots are always real.
accept: the discriminant simplifies to a minus b squared plus four h squared which is a sum of squares so it is never negative and the roots are real
delta is a minus b whole squared plus two h whole squared, at least zero, so real roots
a plus b squared minus four a b is a minus b squared, add four h squared, sum of two squares is non negative
delta a minus b squared plus two h squared avthundi, sum of squares negative kaadu, so roots real
since delta is a sum of two squares it cannot be negative hence the roots are real

steps.why: The whole proof is one identity: (a + b)² − 4ab = (a − b)². Once Δ is a sum of squares it cannot be negative, no matter what a, b, h are — and that is exactly what 'always real' means. Note it is ≥ 0, not > 0: when a = b and h = 0 the two roots are equal, still real.
common_mistakes: Writing (a + b)² − 4ab as (a + b)² and never reaching (a − b)².
Dropping the +4h² or writing it as −4h².
Claiming Δ > 0; it can equal zero (a = b, h = 0), and the roots are still real.
